# Timing and spacing

The **timing** is the same for both balls: 24 frames, same start, same stop. Timing is how long something takes. What is different is the **spacing**: where the ball sits on each frame along the way.

![Three rows of 24 ticks between the same start and stop: heavy with long eases at both ends, light with short eases, and an even row that reads as mechanical](asset:timing_vs_spacing)

- A **heavy** ball is slow to get going and slow to stop. Its positions bunch up at both ends, with wide gaps in the middle.
- A **light** ball gets going and stops almost at once. Its bunches at the ends are short.
- **Even** spacing looks neither heavy nor light. It looks mechanical, like the escalator in Prompt 1.

You set timing on the timeline. You set spacing by where you draw the ball on each frame.

{{deeper}}

**What to keep from this week:** motion looks alive when its timing and spacing carry weight. A drawing does not need to be good to move well.

**Animation is not drawing that moves.** It is arranging time, and the drawings are how you get at it. That is why this course opens on a ball and not on a character. Take away everything a viewer could admire in the artwork, and what is left is the hard part. If a ball convinces someone it is made of something, that is craft, not talent.

**For the rest of the course,** nearly every note on your work will be about one of these two words, timing or spacing. An animator can make an object look heavier or lighter without changing the drawing, and without changing how long it takes.
